title: BABYLON DRESSED LIKE DESIRE: Why Revelation Portrays Corrupt Power as a Prostitute—and Why Her Seduction May Be Closer Than You Think
paragraphs: BABYLON DRESSED LIKE DESIRE: Why Revelation Portrays Corrupt Power as a Prostitute—and Why Her Seduction May Be Closer Than You Think
Revelation 17 does not merely show us a wicked woman. It exposes a world that has learned how to make rebellion beautiful, compromise profitable, and spiritual adultery feel completely normal.
There is something disturbing about the woman John sees.
Not simply because she is evil.
Because she is beautiful.
She does not crawl out of the darkness looking like a monster.
She arrives dressed in purple and scarlet.
Gold glitters against her body.
Precious stones catch the light.
Pearls announce wealth, status, luxury.
There is a golden cup in her hand.
Kings want her.
Nations drink from her.
The powerful cooperate with her.
And people become intoxicated by what she offers.
Then John sees what is really inside the cup.
And suddenly the beauty becomes horrifying.
Revelation 17 opens with words deliberately designed to disturb us:
“Δεῦρο, δείξω σοι τὸ κρίμα τῆς πόρνης τῆς μεγάλης…”
Deuro, deixō soi to krima tēs pornēs tēs megalēs…
“Come, I will show you the judgment of the great prostitute…”
The Greek word is πόρνη — pornē.
It means a prostitute.
Then Revelation speaks of πορνεία — porneia, sexual immorality or prostitution.
John is not softening the picture.
He is making it unforgettable.
But this is where we must read Revelation carefully.
The woman is not presented merely to condemn sexual sinners, and Revelation 17 is certainly not permission to despise women or people trapped in sexual sin.
The woman is a symbol.

The chapter itself eventually tells us that she represents “the great city” exercising dominion over the kings of the earth. The sexual imagery therefore becomes prophetic imagery for something much larger: corrupt civilization seducing humanity away from faithfulness to God.
And that changes everything.
Because Babylon's greatest weapon is not simply persecution.
It is seduction.
Think about that.
Satan does not always need to make you hate God.
Sometimes he only needs to give you something you begin to love more than God.
He does not always need to drag someone screaming away from Jesus.
Sometimes all he needs to do is make compromise attractive enough that the person walks away willingly.
That is Babylon.
Babylon smiles.
Babylon offers the cup.
Babylon tells you that everybody is drinking.
Babylon whispers that obedience is too expensive.
Babylon asks why you should remain faithful when compromise could make your life easier.
And perhaps this is why God chose sexual imagery.
Because throughout Scripture, God describes His relationship with His people using the deeply personal language of covenant faithfulness.
Sin is therefore more than breaking regulations.
Idolatry is more than choosing the wrong religious object.
There is betrayal involved.
Something relational has been violated.
Long before John saw Babylon in Revelation, the prophets used similar imagery.
Isaiah cried over Jerusalem:
“How is the faithful city become an harlot!”
The Hebrew is piercing:
אֵיכָה הָיְתָה לְזוֹנָה קִרְיָה נֶאֱמָנָה
ʾÊkhāh hāyetāh lezōnāh qiryāh neʾĕmānāh.
Literally, the shock is something like:
“How has the faithful city become a prostitute?”
But notice what Isaiah immediately connects with that betrayal.
The city that should have been filled with justice had become associated with bloodshed and corruption.
In other words, biblical “prostitution” imagery can expose not only idolatrous worship but social and moral corruption—the betrayal of justice itself.
Ezekiel 16 develops the imagery even further.
God describes Jerusalem as receiving beauty, provision, clothing, jewelry, food, and honor from Him—and then taking those very gifts and turning them toward idolatry.
That is one of the terrifying patterns of Babylon.
It takes gifts from God and teaches us to worship the gifts instead of the Giver.
Beauty becomes an idol.
Money becomes an idol.
Influence becomes an idol.
Sex becomes an idol.
Politics becomes an idol.
Success becomes an idol.
Comfort becomes an idol.
Even ministry can become an idol.
Even knowledge about God can become something we use to avoid actually surrendering to God.
The tragedy is not simply that people possess good things.
The tragedy begins when good things possess people.
That is why Revelation's woman is covered in wealth.
The gold is not the sin.
The pearls are not the sin.
Purple fabric is not the sin.
The horror is what all that splendor conceals.
A golden cup can still contain poison.
That may be one of Revelation 17's most frightening warnings to modern Christians.
We have become very good at judging things by their packaging.
If something is successful, we assume God approves.
If something becomes popular, we assume it must be good.
If everyone celebrates it, we become afraid to question it.
If compromise makes us richer, more comfortable, more accepted, or more powerful, we can become remarkably talented at renaming compromise “wisdom.”
But Babylon has always understood branding.
She knows how to make chains look like jewelry.
She knows how to make slavery feel like freedom.
She knows how to make spiritual adultery feel like self-discovery.
She knows how to make greed sound like ambition.
She knows how to make pride sound like confidence.
She knows how to make revenge sound like justice.
She knows how to make cowardice sound like tolerance.
And she knows how to make surrender to the spirit of the age feel like progress.
This is why the woman rides a beast.
Beauty is sitting on brutality.
Seduction is riding violence.
Luxury is riding domination.
The glamorous surface hides something monstrous underneath.
And eventually John sees something even worse.
The woman is drunk.
Not with ordinary wine.
With blood.
Revelation says she is drunk with the blood of the saints and the witnesses of Jesus.
Now the mask falls.
The system that promised pleasure ultimately devours people who refuse to worship it.
The seductress becomes persecutor.
The cup becomes blood.
The party becomes judgment.

Historically, there are strong reasons many interpreters have understood Babylon in Revelation 17–18 as symbolically evoking imperial Rome. Revelation itself connects the woman with seven mountains and describes her as ruling over kings, while Rome was famously associated with seven hills. The anti-Roman interpretation has ancient Christian roots, although other interpretations have existed and Christians disagree about how the symbol relates to later or future fulfillment.
That historical setting matters.
But stopping with ancient Rome would make Revelation much safer than John intended it to be.
Because Babylon is not merely something Christians are supposed to identify on a map.

Babylon represents a recurring pattern of human civilization organized in arrogant independence from God—a seductive marriage of idolatry, wealth, domination, immorality, injustice, and opposition to God's faithful witnesses.
Babylon can wear different clothes.
The spirit of Babylon says:
You can have the kingdom without the King.
You can have prosperity without holiness.
You can have spirituality without repentance.
You can have influence without integrity.
You can have pleasure without covenant.
You can have Christianity without a cross.
And perhaps the most dangerous version says:
You can have Jesus as Savior without Jesus as Lord.
That is the lie we need to confront personally.
Because it is easy to read Revelation 17 looking for Babylon somewhere “out there.”
Some government.
Some institution.
Some religious organization.
Some economic system.
Some celebrity.
Some future world empire.
Anyone except us.
But Scripture has an uncomfortable habit of turning the mirror around.
What if Babylon's cup is already near your lips?
What if there is something you know Christ has been asking you to surrender—but you keep negotiating?
What if you would rather lose intimacy with God than lose a relationship?
What if you would rather compromise your conscience than lose money?
What if you would rather hide your faith than lose people's approval?
What if pornography has become the secret room you keep locked while publicly telling everyone Jesus owns the house?
What if bitterness has become so familiar that you no longer recognize it as bondage?
What if success matters more to you than holiness?
What if your Christian identity remains visible while your private devotion to Christ is slowly dying?
That is where Revelation stops being an argument about prophecy charts.
It becomes a confrontation.
Babylon is seductive precisely because she rarely introduces herself as Babylon.
She comes disguised as the thing you think you cannot live without.
And eventually every disciple faces the same terrifying question:
If following Jesus costs me what I desperately want, do I still want Jesus?
Sit with that.
Not the version of Christianity that gives you motivational quotations.
Not the Jesus who exists merely to improve your plans.
Not the Christ reconstructed by culture until He never confronts anyone.
Jesus.
The crucified King.
The risen Lord.
The One who forgives sinners and commands them to follow Him.
The One who touches lepers.
The One who receives the broken.
The One who confronted hypocrites.
The One who welcomed repentant sexual sinners without calling their sin righteousness.
The One who carried a cross.
The One who walked out of a grave.
The One before whom Babylon itself will eventually fall.
Do you still want Him?
Because Revelation ultimately presents two radically different women.
Babylon appears as the prostitute.
Later comes the Bride.
One seduces the world.
The other belongs to the Lamb.
One is clothed in extravagant earthly luxury.
The other is prepared for her Bridegroom.
One intoxicates nations.
The other celebrates the marriage supper of the Lamb.
One rides temporary worldly power.
The other belongs eternally to Jesus Christ.
And that means Revelation is asking:
Whose love has your heart?
There is grace hidden even inside that terrifying question.
Because maybe you have already drunk from cups you wish you could put back.
Maybe you compromised.
Maybe you slept with someone you should not have.
Maybe you betrayed your marriage.
Maybe pornography has scarred your mind.
Maybe money became your master.
Maybe ambition consumed years you cannot recover.
Maybe you manipulated people.
Maybe you traded convictions for acceptance.
Maybe you once burned for Christ, but something happened.
A wound.
A disappointment.
A secret sin.
A prayer that seemed unanswered.
And slowly...
almost imperceptibly...
your heart wandered.
Now you read words like prostitute, unfaithfulness, judgment, and something inside you whispers:
“That is me.”
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not end in Revelation 17.
And your story does not have to end in your scandal.
Jesus Christ came for sinners.
Not polished sinners.
Not respectable sinners.
Not people who successfully concealed enough evidence.
Sinners.
At the cross, Christ bore judgment for everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith.
He did not shed His blood because your sin was small.
He shed His blood because His mercy is greater.
The cross does not tell us sin does not matter.
The cross tells us sin mattered enough for the Son of God to die—and that sinners mattered enough to Him that He willingly came to save them.
That is grace.
Not God pretending the betrayal never happened.
God paying the price Himself.
That is why repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is God calling you out of the burning city.
It is mercy shouting:
Come out.
Stop drinking.
Stop pretending.
Stop hiding.
Stop calling bondage freedom.
Stop defending what Jesus died to free you from.
You do not have to clean yourself before approaching Christ.
You come exposed.
You come guilty.
You come exhausted.
You come with shaking hands if necessary.
But you come.
Because Babylon says, “Hide your shame.”
Jesus says, “Bring it into the light.”
Babylon says, “You need more.”
Jesus says, “Come to Me.”
Babylon says, “Sell your soul and you can belong.”
Jesus gave His life so that sinners could become His.
Babylon decorates slavery.
Jesus breaks chains.
Babylon drinks blood.
Jesus gave His own blood.
Do you see the difference?
Babylon consumes her lovers.
Christ dies for His enemies.
Babylon uses people.
Jesus redeems people.
Babylon promises pleasure and eventually gives death.
Jesus calls us to die to ourselves and ultimately gives life.
That is the scandal of grace.
The King whom we betrayed became the sacrifice by which traitors could be forgiven.
So maybe this article did not reach you because you needed another explanation of Revelation.
Maybe you needed a rescue.
Talk to Jesus.
Confess it.
Name it.
Repent.
Ask for help.
Return.
You do not owe strangers the private details of your struggle. But sometimes three honest words can become the moment someone stops suffering alone.
And if Christ has already brought you out of something that once owned you, tell somebody what His grace has done.
Your testimony may become another person's permission to believe that restoration is still possible.
Then think of one person who needs this message.
Not twenty random names.
One person.
The friend who is quietly compromising.
The believer who has grown cold.
The person drowning in shame.
The Christian who knows Bible verses but has slowly fallen in love with the world.
The unbeliever who assumes Christianity is nothing more than religious people condemning broken people.
Send this privately if that would be wiser.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty.
Because someone in your circle may desperately need to discover that Jesus still receives repentant sinners.
There may come a night when Babylon's cup looks beautiful again.
Come back and remember what was inside it.
The purpose is not merely to build an audience.
It is to keep putting Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and the Gospel of Jesus Christ where people can encounter it.
There is also another way to help this ministry continue and expand.

Scripture teaches that Gospel ministry may legitimately receive material support; Paul wrote that those proclaiming the Gospel may receive their living through Gospel work. Scripture also insists that Christian giving must not be manipulated: a believer gives willingly, not “under compulsion.”
So this invitation is not a purchase of God's favor.
It cannot buy grace.
It cannot buy salvation.
It does not make God love you more.
Supporting Gospel work can glorify God when it rises from a willing heart that desires His truth to spread.
But the merchandise is not the heart of this invitation.
Jesus is.
The Gospel is.
People are.
The exhausted believer who needs encouragement is.
The prodigal quietly reading at 2:00 in the morning is.
The person ashamed of yesterday who needs to discover that Christ still offers a tomorrow is.
Pray.
Share.
Save these messages.
Invite others to follow.
Put truth into circulation.
Because somewhere behind another screen may be a human being standing with Babylon's cup in one hand and unbearable emptiness in the other.
And perhaps one faithful share will put the Gospel in front of them before they take another drink.
Revelation 17 is frightening.
But Babylon does not receive the final word.
Jesus does.
The prostitute falls.
The Lamb reigns.
The kingdoms of this world do not remain forever.
The glitter fades.
The cup empties.
The beast falls.
The marketplace eventually closes.
Every counterfeit kingdom reaches its expiration date.
But Christ remains.
So do not envy Babylon.
Do not fear Babylon.
And do not become Babylon.
Come out of everything that requires you to betray Jesus in order to belong.
Come out of the secret compromise.
Come out of the double life.
Come out of the bitterness.
Come out of the addiction.
Come out of the worship of money.
Come out of the desperate hunger for human approval.
Come out of the beautiful lie.
There is a better Bridegroom.
There is a better Kingdom.
There is a better feast.
There is a better city.
There is a better ending.
His name is Jesus Christ.
And when He takes hold of a ruined story, yesterday's scandal does not have authority to write tomorrow's final sentence.
Babylon may decorate your chains with gold—but Jesus still knows how to break them.
